name: Desiccated beef testicle supplements

lead: These are capsules or powders made from dried beef testicle, taken by people seeking higher testosterone, more muscle and a better physique. The thinking is that eating an organ supports the same organ in the eater, an idea from the older tradition of organotherapy.

Proponents propose that nutrients or hormone-related compounds in the organ pass on benefit. The idea descends from Brown-Sequard's 1889 testicular extracts, which did not yield active amounts of testosterone and whose effects are now thought to be placebo. One trial of an organ-based supplement with testosterone as its condition is registered as active, with no results found.

paras: People take them as daily capsules, often as part of a broader organ-meat or ancestral-style diet and alongside training. Users typically take them for weeks and judge by energy, gym progress and bloodwork.
The sources reviewed describe no safety data for these products. Wikipedia notes that many historical glandular extracts were promoted without systematic evidence of safety and efficacy.

angle.text: Dried beef testicle capsules are taken on the idea that eating an organ supports the same organ, aiming for higher testosterone and more muscle. The idea traces to 1889 organ-extract experiments whose effects are now attributed to placebo.

lead: Desiccated beef testicle supplements are dried, usually encapsulated, preparations of bovine testicular tissue sold as dietary supplements. People take them in ancestral-diet and testosterone-focused circles with the aim of supporting male vitality, training performance and a more muscular, leaner physique; the products are promoted on a "like supports like" idea that eating an organ benefits the same organ in the consumer.

The idea has a long lineage. Organotherapy used animal glands and tissues as treatments and contributed to modern endocrinology, although many preparations were poorly standardised or promoted without systematic evidence.[1] In 1889 the physiologist Charles-Edouard Brown-Sequard reported injecting himself with testicular extract; his claims were dismissed by contemporaries, and the positive responses are now thought to have been placebo.[2]

A registered 2025 study of an organ-supplement company's product package lists testosterone as its condition; no completed clinical trials of the oral supplements have reported results.[3] In the US, dietary supplements are regulated as foods under the 1994 DSHEA, and labels may carry structure/function claims with an FDA disclaimer.[4]

paras: The supplements are made from dried bovine testicular tissue, typically sold as capsules or powder and often alongside other organ preparations such as liver or heart. Closely related is the culinary tradition of eating bull testicles, known in North America as Rocky Mountain oysters, prairie oysters or calf fries, and in Spain and Latin America as criadillas or huevos de toro; Wikipedia notes that many people consider the dish an aphrodisiac.[5]
Wikipedia's organ meat article reports a recent revival of offal eating in parts of Europe, partly through awareness of its nutritional content and promotion by fitness influencers.[6]

Organotherapy, also called opotherapy, aimed to replace absent or insufficient internal secretions with organ preparations.[1] In 1889, at age 72, Brown-Sequard told the Societe de Biologie in Paris that injections of testicular fluid from guinea pigs and dogs rejuvenated him, and thousands of men tried the therapy.[2] Endocrinologist Robert Greenblatt argued that it could not have worked, because the testes do not store their hormones, and later experiments found that the method did not yield active amounts of testosterone.[2] Standardised hormone treatments largely replaced crude organ preparations.[1]

Under the US Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, supplements are treated as food. Manufacturers do not need government approval before sale and are responsible for confirming safety, and the FDA can act against unsafe products. Labels cannot claim to treat disease but may carry structure/function claims with a disclaimer.[4]

No studies found with published results. A registered study, NCT07256639, evaluates a company's whole-food organ supplement package on men's health with testosterone as the listed condition; it enrolled 100 participants, started in October 2025 and is listed as active, not recruiting.[3]

timeline.event: Brown-Sequard reports self-injection of animal testicular extract in Paris; the claims are dismissed by contemporaries [2].
George Redmayne Murray treats myxoedema with sheep-thyroid extract, spurring interest in other organ extracts [1].
